subsubtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS IN LETTER SIGNED BY GOVERNMENT MINISTERS AND SUPPORTERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to seek the permission of the House to move a motion on a subject of urgent and pressing necessity. It relates to the necessity that the government immediately implement the recommendations contained in a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), dated February 3, 1982, signed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister of State (Mr. Joyal) and certain Members of Parliament, which urged the government to proceed with the immediate creation of two new programs to create employment in key sectors of the economy, by stimulating domestic housing construction and by launching a program to enable private enterprise to hire young Canadians.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That the House strongly endorse the position of the authors of the Begin-Joyal letter when they wrote: "Mr. Prime Minister, we urge you to adopt these measures as soon as possible because we are convinced that they are necessary
right now."

subsubtopic: TRAINING COURSES FOR YOUNG MINERS-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Mining Association of Canada and many other experts have predicted that by 1985 there will be a severe shortage of several thousand skilled mine workers which will largely arise because of the major coal and oil sands projects slated for western Canada. However, Canadian mining companies are presently laying off hundreds of their youngest employees who are low on the seniority scale because of the current economic depression. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
That the Minister of State for Mines, in collaboration with her colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, be requested to implement immediately an emergency training program so that, instead of sitting around with nothing to do, young mine workers might be placed in accelerated skills-training courses under the supervision of experienced mine workers at their present places of employment, and that UIC benefits normally payable to those young persons be used to finance the cost of such training.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and public importance, and hope that in view of the comments of the Solicitor General we might have unanimous consent. All Canada views with disgust and dismay the announcement by mass murderer Clifford Olson that the sensibilities of Canadians may soon again be abused by his demented memoirs in book and serial form, the object of which would be to further enrich this mass murderer and rapist for his crimes at the expense of the people of Canada. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Soviet Jewish dissident Anatoly Shcharansky has been unjustly held for over six months in solitary confinement and on low rations by the Soviet authorities in direct contravention of basic human rights and of Soviet obligations under the Helsinki Accord to respect the fundamental freedoms of conscience and religion. In view of this injustice and the plea of Mr. Shcharansky's wife that politicians in the west take up her husband's cause, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker):
That this House call on the Soviet Union to live up to its obligation under the Helsinki Accord and immediately release Anatoly Shcharansky from detention.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION PLANNING TASK FORCE REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. In March, 1981, the minister said, "The mobilization planning task force is expected to report later this year"-that is, later in 1981. In November, 1981, the minister said, "The work of the mobilization plan task force is not yet finalized."
At the January, 1982, Conference of the Defence Associations the minister referred to the mobilization plan and said, " ... a number of options and possibilities have been examined, and they are being examined even now, as I speak."
Would the minister tell the House exactly when Canadians can expect to see some results from this drawn-out, procrastinating process?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION PLANNING TASK FORCE REPORT
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Victoria has just pointed out, Madam
Speaker, the whole question of mobilization in Canada has been under review for about a year and a half now. A task force is still carrying out this study in an attempt to reach a conclusion. There are several options, of course, as the hon. member said. Whatever they may be there is a price tag on all those options and for the time being we are trying to refine upon-if I may use the word-the conclusions with respect to a mobilization plan which should be ready within a few weeks.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the problem is that the minister is using the lack of a mobilization plan as the reason for turning down every other initiative which is put to him.
The report of the Senate Sub-committee on National Defence which was tabled yesterday contained among its recommendations that the government begin production immediately of a new white paper on defence, that the number of regular force personnel be increased to 92,000 by 1987, and that the Canadian forces CAST commitment be reviewed. When will the government do anything about any of these recommendations?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: SENATE SUBCOMMITTEE REPORT RECOMMENDATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we are taking into consideration all proposals from the various well-known and respected groups, such as, of course, the Senate. We have taken some action on some of the resolutions which were made during the last Canadian Defence Association convention. Last year, the Standing Committee of the House of Commons on External Affairs and National Defence made several proposals on mobilization, unification, and the reserves. We have taken action on all these proposals. I can give the hon. member information on what has been done as a result of these recommendations, what has been implemented to date, and what will be implemented in the future.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S STATEMENT ON PROJECTS TO INCREASE GROWTH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Today is the third anniversary of the November 12 budget. In the past 90 days more than 168,000 Canadians have been laid off. During that same period of time Canadians representing every region of the country and virtually every occupation, and indeed finally Canadians in the back benches of the Liberal Party, have called for changes in the government's financial direction.
On Wednesday the minister indicated that he was prepared to consider "innovative projects intended to produce growth." Will the minister now tell us what those projects are?
February 12, 1982

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's interest in this subject. Obviously members of the House are concerned about unemployment levels and lay-offs. I have stated in the House that within the current fiscal framework the government will undertake specific projects, and I have replied to the Leader of the Opposition that when any decisions are taken on this matter I will ensure that the decisions are announced, but decisions have not yet been taken.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 33 per cent of the forestry workers in British Columbia are out of work. Fifty thousand auto workers are out of work. More than
480,000	young Canadians are out of work. How much longer do the people of this country-cumulatively almost a million and a half unemployed Canadians-have to wait before this government demonstrates some concern by bringing in new programs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member believes a number of specific new programs would solve the problems of these particular groups. I believe he is misleading them into that belief because it is my view that unless we succeed in bringing down the level of prices in this country we will not be able to solve the problem of unemployment. That is why I believe we must assume a firm anti-inflationary posture in order to create the conditions for renewed growth and for employment creation in the country. That is the basic thrust of the budget, and that is the basic policy of the government.

subtopic: REASONS FOR POSITION TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT
REASONS FOR POSITION TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the past the minister has been fond of drawing our attention to the international situation. I point out to him that even a conservative administration like that of Ronald Reagan in the United States indicated last week that it is no longer preoccupied with the level of budget deficits. In Europe some time ago the government of France, and just some ten days ago the government of West Germany, announced major new initiatives to stimulate their economies because they are concerned about the people in their countries. They will not stand back and watch millions more become unemployed.
Does the failure of the Government of Canada to act at this point really demonstrate that, in terms of its ideas, it is either intellectually bankrupt or, in terms of its concerns about the people of Canada, morally indifferent? Or, frankly, is it both?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance

Madam Speaker, just to comment on the hon. member's reference to the policy of the United States government, what is causing great concern in the United

States and elsewhere is the projected level of the deficit in that country. Everybody seems to understand that if that deficit is maintained and grows larger, it will limit or remove any possibility of bringing down interest rates in the United States. Why have short-term interest rates gone up in the United States in the last week? It is partly because of the concerns which have been expressed about the projected level of the budget deficit in the United States.
If the hon. member is serious about creating jobs in Canada he will be as dedicated as I am to doing everything possible to bring down interest rates. He ignores that problem in all his questions because he seems to believe we can reach solutions in Canada and forget about rising prices and rising inflation.

Naturally, it is not printed the day before. By that announcement, today's Order Paper reflects two changes. It reflects a change on page

In order to found my argument that neither the government House leader nor the Table has that right I will have to refer to the standing orders. The Chair referred to one of the Standing Orders yesterday, namely Standing Order 18. It reads:

There is a clear distinction. This perhaps comes close to touching on the ruling of the Chair yesterday, but I am focusing my argument on my right as an opposition member in the name of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to have that motion on the Order Paper.

motions will be debated next Friday, assuming, of course, that the government House leader does not change his mind again and put the allotted day somewhere else.

On any day or days appointed for the consideration of any business under the provisions of this Standing Order,

Under the terms of Standing Order 58(5) twenty-five days are allotted to the business of supply in each year. Although technically the business under discussion is government business-

February 12, 1982
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
Why "technically?" It is because supply is government business. Why "technically?" Because technically the government can deal with the item under supply. It is my submission that this is the very reason for the existence of Standing Order 58(2), which reads:

Madam Speaker, I will not be too long, I just want to finalize the remarks I began to make just before we broke for lunch.
As I see it what you have before you, Madam Speaker, are two questions. One is whether or not the text of a proposed motion to be dealt with on an allotted day should appear on the Order Paper and Notices. I think there is sufficient argument before you now to enable you to make a decision on that without too much difficulty.
The second question is probably more important, both in terms of the immediate problem which has confronted us over the past two days, but also in terms of how we might deal with matters such as this in the future. I think it requires a considerable amount of thought. I know you will do that, and I hope other members will do likewise because this question is of vital importance.
As I see it, having thought about the matter over lunch, the question is whether an allotted day is in fact government business and therefore subject to the normal ordering of government business within the latitude given to the House leader for the government or whether the House leader has to deal technically in a different way with the calling of House business for an allotted day than he would for any other day.
I would submit there is no question that an allotted day is different from a normal government business day. The primary difference is the difference which my colleague, the hon. member for Yukon indicated, about which he was questioned by you. In other words, the difference is simply that an opposition member on that particular day is given the primary responsibility for moving a motion, but on all other counts the day remains a government day.
I want to say to you that what my wishes might be are of little consequence. How I might like it to be does not matter
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
very much. It is how it is that makes the difference in a situation such as this, and whether we want to change it.
It is quite clear, if one looks at issues of Order Paper and Notices going back as far as one might want to look, that even an allotted day appears under government orders. I would suggest, by virtue of that and given the references in Beau-chesne to allotted days-albeit allotted days are referred to in the technical sense as a government order-it would appear historically that they have been treated as a government order for the purpose of ordering business of the House. Therefore, it must be decided whether the government has to do anything specific in order to change the government orders.
I looked very carefully at that over lunch and I came to the conclusion that, although I would prefer the government being required to move motions to alter the orders of the day as it would want to alter them from time to time-and I want to differentiate between orders of the day as they are set out in the Standing Orders and the orders to be called within any specific order-by virtue of that fact, orders to be called within any specific order are at the discretion of the government House leader and that the government House leader may, if he wishes, or may not if he so desires, call any order that appears legitimately on the Order Paper and Notices.
Therefore, I come to the conclusion somewhat reluctantly that the method of determining whether an allotted day would be called or set off to another time remains within the purview of the government House leader.
What does not remain within the purview of the government House leader is whether there will be allotted days. That is quite clear. It is set out in the Standing Orders that there will be a certain number of allotted days to be called during a specific period of the sittings of the House, and that can be altered only with unanimous consent.
So I suggest that on the one hand we have it quite clearly before us that allotted days in the specified number must be made available to the opposition, but the determination of which days will be allotted remains the purview of the government. If it is to be considered that the allocation of that allotted day is government business, then the government House leader can either call that on the day he designates or he can change the day. In this instance I think he chose the latter, for whatever reason, and however much I would like to argue he cannot, I think he can and I know he did.
Therefore, I submit that on the first question, yes, I agree wholeheartedly with the House leader for the official opposition, the motion should have appeared with the one caveat mentioned earlier, that is, whether or not the dating of the motion is to be given consideration. I would urge that it not be found to be of importance in terms of whether the motion should appear on the Order Paper, but by the same token I would argue that for the balance, undesirable though the procedure might be, it would appear to me to be consistent with practice and with the laws as they pertain to the running of Parliament.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the NDP House leader in what I take to be some support for the position taken by the government House leader yesterday. I think it exemplifies some things which have bothered me, as a new Member of Parliament, about the functioning of Parliament and a certain lack of precision, and the possibilities arising out of that for the philosophy we hold to sort of take over and take us to a particular perspective.
I think the counterargument to the NDP House leader is really found in pages 3 to 7 of Beauchesne where it clearly tells us that the rules of the House are to protect us from the tyranny of a majority. We have used that phrase on many occasions in debate related to orders, but yesterday we faced a government decision to change the orders of the day, and there has been some argument presented in relation to that. However, the perspective presented by the NDP House leader, and I think by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) relates to the use of Standing Order 18(2), which says that:
Government orders shall be called and considered in such sequence as the government determines.
I suggest to you, Madam Speaker, on first reading that looks like a fairly precise paragraph, but its interpretation hinges on the word "determines." If we consider that the cabinet has an untrammelled right, then it is conceivable the government House leader can rise on a point of order in the middle of a debate and change the orders of the day, and move abruptly from debate for which members have prepared themselves to one for which they have not. That is the principle upon which the government and NDP House leaders have essentially based their argument, that a small group of people in cabinet have an untrammelled right to step on the remaining 250 members' rights to advance their arguments.
Yesterday, Madam Speaker, the government acted on that principle, that they had the right to take away an allotted day, not a day given to an opposition party, but in principle a day which had been determined in advance by the government as being available to any and all members who were or might be opposed to government policies, or who might like the opportunity to indicate whether or not they were so opposed.
Members of this House who had arranged their schedules, put their notes together and had their arguments ready were denied by that move the opportunity to express their collective will. As a member of the Conservative Party of Canada standing here today, Madam Speaker, I would have liked that allotted day to have occurred, I would have liked to have had at five o'clock that vote in which the government, the 30 or 35 members of cabinet, sought the approval of the House for their economic policy, and I would have liked those who were opposed to have had the opportunity to stand up and so indicate. If the government had fallen, Madam Speaker, we would have been in a general election and the voters of this country could have determined whether or not they were in accord with government policy.

It is the other part of the question, that the motion could only be removed from the Order Paper with unanimous consent. Of course, there was not unanimous consent.
It is well to put this debate into the context of what the House intended by allotted days. It is important to bear in mind what exactly the Standing Order had intended by these allotted days. Anyone who was here prior to 1965 when these Standing Orders were brought in on a provisional basis will know that we had at that time the committee of supply. The committee of supply was a committee of the whole House before which all the estimates were examined without regard to time. The estimates were brought before the committee of supply, the committee of the whole House, and it was the opposition which determined when the estimates would be passed by the committee of supply and returned back to the House.
I agree that was not an entirely satisfactory procedure because it sometimes caused serious problems. I remember one occasion when it resulted in the government not being able to meet the public service payroll and having to resort to Governor General's warrants. Everybody realized something had to be done to replace that procedure.
The procedure which replaced it, allotted days under the provision of Standing Order 58, is not entirely satisfactory. It is well for the House and the Chair to note that these Standing Orders we are now operating under were in fact passed by the invocation of closure in 1968. The reason the government had to invoke closure to bring in these Standing Orders in 1968 was that many members of the House at that time were very concerned with what would happen to the right of the House to hold the government accountable, particularly on the way it managed the budget.
If you look at Standing Order 58(14), you will find, I think, that it makes the point very well which I am trying to make. All estimates are now referred to a committee. Standing Order 58(14) says:
Each such committee shall consider and shall report, or shall be deemed to have reported, the same back to the House not later than May 31 in the then current fiscal year.
That is why these 25 allotted days are critically important to the House. The 25 days were not picked out of a hat. It was based upon the experience of the House and the number of days that the committee of supply dealt with estimates. In other words, in place of the estimates being referred to the Committee of the Whole House, we were given the 25 allotted days.
Of course, within the 25 allotted days, provision was made for a number of these days to be used for non-confidence
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
motions. These non-confidence motions replaced the motions that were brought in previously under the old supply procedure whereby no notice was required and no notice was given. When the opposition stood up to bring in a motion under supply which was non-confidence in the government, all the ministers had to sit there wondering which one would be the target of that particular motion. That was the procedure. There was some dissatisfaction and the government felt that it was not really the way to run the House. There was agreement that there had to be another procedure to replace that one.
The hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) said it is worth examining this whole question. I also think it is worth examining. I think, Madam Speaker, that you would be well advised to urge the government House leader to convene a meeting or make a reference to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization so that the House can be officially seized of this question and thereby enable us to examine the Standing Orders in the context of the experience that we have had since the present Standing Orders were adopted.
I repeat that it is my submission that agreement was reached on the allocation of an allotted day, and once agreement was reached, that allotted day would be a votable motion, one of the motions of non-confidence provided for in the 25 allotted days, and once the motion in accordance with our agreement was tabled, it then ceased to be government business. At that point in time it was out of the control of the government. It could only be changed by unaninous consent of the House.
I respectfully submit to you that that is the crux of the argument. The government House leader stood in his place yesterday at three o'clock and unilaterally did what he did not have the right to do under the Standing Orders: to change what had been unanimously agreed to by his colleagues. The process was already in play by virtue of the required notice appearing on the Order Paper and the motion, which should have been the subject of debate today, already having been filed by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: NOTICES OF SUPPLY PROCEEDINGS PURSUANT TO STANDING ORDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think I can be very brief in speaking to this point of order. There are one or two matters which have been raised and require some response.
If I understood the position being put forward by the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader correctly, part of his argument, which was technical and perhaps not central to what he was arguing, was that since the references to allotted days appeared in the Order Paper section known as notices, that made it somehow less compelling than if it had appeared elsewhere in the Order Paper. I am sure it was only momentarily overlooked by the parliamentary secretary but I think it is important that the House understand and recall that motions for concurrence on estimates are also listed in the same place and stay in their same place until they are called. That part of the Order Paper is an integral part of the Order Paper.

February 12. 1982
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
If that suggestion was indeed made by the parliamentary secretary, that the language relating to the allotted day on that part of the Order Paper might be somewhat less compelling than if it had appeared elsewhere, I would contest that. That part of the Order Paper is unquestionably an integral part of the Order Paper. It is there to fulfil the requirements of the Standing Orders which require notice in matters relating to supply, whether it has to do with a motion for concurrence in estimates or whether it has to do with acts related to allotted days.
The second matter to which I want to turn my attention deals with the very alarming precedent which we may be establishing here. The events of the last two days, the matter which was raised yesterday and the matter which was raised by my colleague today, create a very real danger of censorship, which is something that runs against the very grain of the rights of an opposition, and consequently, the rights of Parliament. One serious result of a continuation of the events that occurred yesterday would be that once a government became aware of the nature of a notice that had been filed for an allotted day, if it took exception to that particular notice or was fearful of not being able to carry the House on a motion of that kind-which we suspect was the case yesterday-it could be in a position to act in a way which would deny the opposition the right that had been established for it to proceed with that motion or action. That is clearly censorship and an addition to the limitations put upon the capacity of the whole Parliament generally and specifically of the official opposition, of other opposition parties and any other Members of Parliament who might disagree with a particular item of government business. This is another limitation upon the capacity of members of the House of Commons to control the actions and decisions of the government. As these limitations continue to accumulate, we will have no parliamentary system left in any honest sense of the word.
The point which was raised by my seatmate and colleague, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), again speaks to the question of (potential censorship. If the practice which occurred today, whfah was probably inadvertent, continues, not only is there tntf capacity of censorship on the right of an opposition to raise a question, there is the censorship of the very right of that opposition to have the language of the motions that it intends to have introduced stand on the Order Paper of the House of Commons.
The more important matter which 1 would like to deal with was raised explicitly by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette). He raised the critical and fundamental question freshly today in the argument of this point of order and it concerns the question of to whom the allotted days belong. Do they belong to the government? Are they subject to absolute control by the government, or do they belong to the official opposition whose primary responsibility is to keep control of the government and stop it from excess? I noted what the hon. member for York East said, and if I heard him correctly, I believe he said that allotted days "are indeed government days." The hon. member nods that that is his view. I disagree
with that view strenuously. Not only does it run against all the traditions and understanding we have had in the House, it very clearly runs against what is spelled out in Beauchesne and what is spelled out in the Standing Orders of the House of Commons. To accept the view that allotted days are indeed government days is to extend even more the control of the government of the day over the House of Commons.
All of us who have been students of this place and believe in the importance of parliamentary democracy know that one of the grave dangers which has developedTtver the years is that the power of individual Members of Parliament has diminished and the power of the government has increased. We now have virtually no means to control a government which is pursuing a policy which is unpopular with the majority of members of the House and bad for the country. Powers which used to exist here and used to reside with oppositions here have been stripped away one by one. As my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has indicated, one of the most dramatic changes in the powers of individual Members of Parliament was enforced by closure, because Parliament would not willingly have accepted that. The extraordinary recourse to closure had to be used. We may very well be on the brink of even one more major limitation upon the capacity of Parliament to do our basic job, which is to control, in the name of the people of Canada, the executive members of the government.
My colleague, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), made a very important point. It was not simply members on the opposition side of the House of Commons who were interested in being heard on the matter which would have been debated today. Undoubtedly there were members on the government side who wanted to be heard, some of whom may well have wanted to vote with the opposition against the government. Indeed, I believe it was for that reason the matter was withdrawn.
However, the point is not limited to what was denied Parliament today. The point has to do with what might be denied Parliament permanently, and what might be denied Parliament permanently is the opportunity to use this instrument to assert control of the executive by individual members of the House of Commons on any side of the House and of any party.
The hon. member for York East has quoted Beauchesne Citation 478( 1). He quoted it for a third time. The relevant part is the following:
Although technically the business under discussion is government business, motions given precedence on these allotted days may be moved only by members in opposition to the government. To this extent, there is a distinction between the business of supply and other government business with respect to S.O. 18.
The important word here is "technically", and what the language of Citation 478( I) makes abundantly clear is that for a technical reason it might be grouped under government business, but the reality is that it belongs not to the government but to the opposition. That is why the word "technically" is there. There is no other explanation for the presence of that
February 12, 1982

word, and the use of the word "technically" is designed explicitly to underline the fact that the control of allotted days rests not with the government, which controls everything else, but with the opposition, which controls little more than this ability to hold the government to account through the use of allotted days.
Your Honour will be aware of Standing Order 58(12), which reads as follows:
On any day or days appointed for the consideration of any business under the provisions of this Standing Order, that order of business shall have precedence over all other government business in such sitting or sittings.
There can be no doubt that today had been appointed. The argument has been put that not only was the day appointed, but also that by the filing of the notice it was consummated. There can be no question about that. There can be no question of the meaning of Standing Order 58(12), but the matter I wanted to address directly had to do with the question of to whom does an allotted day belong. Does it belong to the opposition, as all our practices and Beauchesne make clear, or does it belong to the government to be dismissed at the government's whim?
I will repeat myself in closing. The word "technically" makes it abundantly clear that while for some small technical reason it might be grouped under the heading of government business, the clear purport and the clear reason for having the provision here at all is to provide the opposition with an instrument to control the government, and if that were to be denied, that would be one more stripping away of the powers of the opposition and one more reduction of the ability of the people of Canada through their Parliament to control the government.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. It is obvious that what we are entering into here and what we are concerned with is something which is considered very valuable and important not just to the opposition but to all Members of Parliament in terms of our ability to make Parliament function in a manner which would allow it to pass good legislation. We are involved in a very fine balance. That balance is made up of both government members and opposition members, and anything that would detract from that balance may well have a very serious effect on the ability of Parliament to function.
I think it is important that we look at a few of the things which relate to this particular issue and particularly the one we are talking about here, the orders of the day. 1 refer to Citation 275 of Beauchesne at page 89 which talks about the Order Paper and Notices. It says this:
The paper known as Order Paper and Notices is the official agenda printed on the responsibility of the Clerk of the House, containing all the proposed questions set out in accordance with the Standing Orders. All the proposed proceedings of the House are recorded in abbreviated form in that paper. To add to, or suppress from it. any proposal which the House has ordered would constitute a serious infringement on the priveleges of the House of Commons.
I think that is a large part of what we are concerned about here today. Perhaps, in fact, what is happening is that the opposition is losing its ability to participate in a particular opportunity which has, by precedent and by history, been provided to it.
Our concern is that if we cannot work within this particular framework and have this type of opportunity made available to us, we will end up with a serious loss of our opportunity to serve this House and our constituents as well.
In order to look at that breach of privilege referred to in Beauchesne one must look back at the very foundation of privilege, and again I refer to Beauchesne. According to Beauchesne, the privileges of Parliament afe rights which are absolutely necessary for the due execution of its powers, and they are enjoyed by individual members because the House cannot perform its functions without unimpeded use of the services of its members. We can see that the balance 1 referred to earlier is a fine balance based on the privileges of the House. It is based on the format the House has laid out for itself and the rules and guidelines under which it must perform. We obviously feel that balance was changed yesterday by an unusual procedure employed by the government House leader.
The final point that 1 want to make was raised earlier by my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) who talked about the principles of parliamentary law. These

February 12, 1982
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
are set out on page 3 of Beauchesne's fifth edition in part as follows:
To protect a minority and restrain the improvidence or tyranny of a majority; to secure the transaction of public business in an orderly manner; to enable every Member to express his opinions within limits necessary to preserve decorum-
That sets out the guidelines, certain rules and regulations that are designed to allow Parliament and Members of Parliament to function in a real and positive way.
When we have such things as allotted days set out on the Order Paper, it is for a certain purpose, that purpose being that the opposition can organize its debate, its methods, and its approach to various levels of government business. It is a very serious and important opportunity for the opposition to criticize the government.
In regard to this point of order I think it is essential that we look at how important these provisions are and how necessary they are to the opposition and, in fact, to all members of the House of Commons in order that they may perform their duties and make certain that the laws and legislation passed by the House are passed in accordance with certain procedures and forms.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
maintopic: NOTICES OF SUPPLY PROCEEDINGS PURSUANT TO STANDING ORDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to add a word or two in response to the remarks of the acting House leader for the New Democratic Party and my colleague the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper). It has been the practice in this House for the government House leader to announce the business of the House for some period of time and for that to be recorded in the orders of the day. Yesterday we came to something which was unprecedented, a change made in the orders of the day by the government House leader.
I would ask you to address yourself, Madam Speaker, to the way in which the orders of the day were changed-not that they were changed but the way in which they were changed. I would like to refer you to page 89 of Beauchesne's fifth edition, Citation 276 which reads as follows:
A motion to proceed to another government order may be moved only by the government House leader (or a member acting on his behalf).
Yesterday an unprecedented change in government business was made by the government because of a certain fear of a vote. That change was not made by any motion offered by the government House leader or anyone acting on his behalf, but simply by the government House leader making the comment that he was changing it.
I think what we on this side are after is some finality. People ask us how we conduct the business of government, what we do day in, day out, how we organize our weeks and our months. We have to be able to tell the people who send us here that there is some certainty in this House. The certainty that we on this side are looking for is the certainty of government orders.
When government orders which have already been set into the orders of the day by the government House leader, by his statement-and until now we have taken his word for it- those words are set in stone, set in the Journals or set in Hansard, and surely we are owed the courtesy of a motion
which is part of the business of the House, rather than an offhand comment such as we got yesterday from the government House leader, if there is to be a change.
Citation 276 of Beauchesne's says "A motion to proceed to another government order may be moved-," and it seems to me that infers that there will be a motion to change the business of the day; something which can be considered, which is in writing, which has formality to it and would be voted upon. Perhaps we would not have won the vote on the motion, but at least it should have been moved by the government House leader or by the deputy government House leader. Neither of those events occurred, Madam Speaker.
In your ruling, Madam Speaker, I would ask you to address the question of whether it was done properly by just announcing it in an offhand manner and whether, when we reach government orders today or any other day, we are to be subjected to such a comment in the middle of the business of the day. When the government House leader has set the business for the day, is he going to be forced-and I say, forced-by the rules which govern this House, forced by tradition, by Beauchesne, by the Standing Orders and orders of the day, to bring in a motion. It is like any motion and the mover and seconder lose control over it once it is within the purview of the House. I suggest that when the orders of the day come within the purview of the House, then a motion must be introduced, seconded and debated.

Madam Speaker, one could be left to draw the conclusion that somehow there is a conspiracy on the part of the government to deny hon. members of the opposition a copy of the bill as amended in committee. If in fact there was a problem in getting the reprinted version to members as quickly as possible, it had nothing to do with the government; it is the responsibility of the law clerk.
If we look at Standing Order 75(3), it is quite clear that we have complied with what is necessary in order for report stage of any bill to be reported by a standing committee. It indicates that it "shall not be taken into consideration prior to 48 hours following the presentation of the said report, unless otherwise ordered by the House". member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), before making a decision. He has certainly had that opportunity now. speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. DEANS-DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF BILL C-78

speechtext: If Madam Speaker wishes me to take that as a question, I am in your hands. I am not blaming anybody. I am simply pointing out what are the facts. Certainly the government knows what took place at committee, because government members were on the committee and were familiar with what in fact took place. It would not need the latest version to draw whatever amendments it felt were necessary, because it would have the original version and its members would have been at committee to know what in fact took place there. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a short interjection which I think relates to the previous argument in the sense that each of us in the house is equal and that independents, and perhaps even government backbenchers, would like to move amendments to the bill. subtopic: MR. DEANS-DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF BILL C-78
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot sit here and allow the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) to say that the government is not responsible. The government is responsible for every aspect of presenting a bill, right from the beginning to the end. If the government is not responsible, who is? Is it the opposition? We had nothing to do with it. The man is in such a jam that he is ignoring things which are elementary. It is elementary that government has responsibility for every phase of a bill. speechtext:
1.	Does Petro-Canada require social insurance numbers on applications for its credit cards and, if so, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: USE OF SIN NUMBERS BY PETRO-CANADA
speechtext:
1 am informed by the Department of Justice and Petro-Canada as follows:
1.	No. Petro-Canada is presently revising its application forms for credit cards and will not require that social insurance numbers be supplied by applicants.
2.	In response to public concern about the use of the social insurance number within the federal government, the Minister of Justice, on May 23, 1980, extended the terms of reference of a study into the use of the social insurance number, being conducted by the Privacy Commissioner, to include the use of the number by those federal government departments and institutions which are subject to the provisions of Part IV of the Canadian Human Rights Act. This includes all departments and 62 agencies of the federal government.
The Privacy Commissioner's report on the use of the social insurance number in Canada, tabled in the House of Commons on March 31, 1981, by the Minister of Justice, thoroughly documents the use of the number by the federal government. The report indicates that the SIN is used most often by departments and agencies when there is a legal requirement to provide it, such as under the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Canada Pension Plan and the Income Tax Act. It is also used to identify individuals involved in financial assistance programs administered by the federal government and as an employee identification number.
While the report indicates that there is fairly widespread use of the SIN by federal government departments and agencies, it concludes that this is not a matter which should cause concern. This conclusion is based on the primary finding of the report: that the use of the social insurance number does not, in and of itself, pose a threat to the privacy of individuals. The major perceived problem associated with widespread use of the social insurance number is its potential for use as a data-linkage device. The Privacy Commissioner found no evidence that the SIN has been misused as a data-linkage device. Moreover, as data-linkage can now be accomplished by the use of other identifiers, such as name, address and birth date, reducing the use of the SIN would not be an effective method of combating the problems associated with this practice.
Finally, the report points out that there are positive factors associated with the use of a single identifying number. These

February 12, 1982
Order Paper Questions

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' NOTICES OF MOTIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to change the automatic deduction of one hundred dollars for medical expenses and charitable donations, to an automatic deduction of one hundred dollars for medical expenses, with all charitable donations being deductible from the total income on which tax payable is calculated.
He said: Madam Speaker, if there is one thing I can be thankful for to the NDP today, all five of them, it is that they have brought, by their motion and through the efforts of the opposition and government whips, members into the House to listen to this debate which is of some considerable importance. 1 want to thank hon. members for staying. This is a moment which shall live in my memory as a parliamentarian. Having said that, they have my permission to leave if they wish, since it is Friday afternoon. This is private members' hour and one knows what usually happens to private members' motions. 1

February 12, 1982

think it is very important that we advance private members' motions from time to time.
This is a motion which hopefully is designed to improve the lot of the great army of volunteers in Canada who perhaps do not even know how influential they are, how important they are and what a force for good they are. Thefore, I hope this motion is accepted at least for consideration by the government.
As did the earlier motion of the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche)-which I had the honour to second-I hope this motion will centre public attention on the importance of the recognition government ought to give to the volunteer sector.
I said this is a great army of volunteers, and it is. These unsung heroes service the needs of the country. They might belong to service clubs such as Kiwanis, Rotary or Kinsmen. The men and women in those organizations are all brothers and sisters under the sun. They are the people who go from door to door for the Cancer Society, the Heart Association and other charities. The United Way and the people who contribute to it are a force for good, and they are a mighty force.
In a labour force survey released in January of 1981, Statistics Canada noted that 2.7 million adults worked as volunteers in Canada in the year ending February, 1980. Total volunteer hours worked during that year numbered over 373 million, equivalent to approximately 281,000 person-years of volunteer labour. The then secretary of state and now Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) noted in a speech to the Committee of National Voluntary Organizations in January, 1981, that this labour is equivalent to 75 per cent of the entire federal public service and that if the labour was compensated at the average industrial wage, it would represent a value of $3.5 billion in forgone wages by Canadian volunteers. That is the extent of the work.
Volunteers and the organizations they support are active in virtually every facet of Canadian life. Our 47,000 registered charities provide the vehicles through which a tremendous percentage of our cultural, spiritual, educational and social services are developed and delivered. Hospitals, universities, the Stratford Festival, the YMCA, the Red Cross, UNICEF, the National Ballet and the United Way are all registered charities. The whole concept of universal social and health services was developed by the volunteer sector many years before it was adopted by governments.
Without exception, the cultural and educational institutions we take for granted in this country and elsewhere were started by a few small groups of dedicated volunteers. More importantly, no matter how big they have grown, all these organizations are still run by volunteer boards of directors which raise the funds necessary to keep them going, make the policies that animate their activities and keep them accountable to the communities they serve.
The problem is, however, like everything else in this world, these services have been growing rapidly, and the costs of
Income Tax
providing them have been growing even more rapidly. In response to rising costs, voluntary organizations are becoming even more imaginative in terms of searching for ways to raise the additional and necessary funds. Unfortunately, all their efforts have not been successful, and that is why we hear from time to time of the precarious state of, for example, the Winnipeg Symphony. We hear concerns about United Way campaigns getting over the top, and sometimes they do not. We hear about cutbacks in services at the Sick Children's Hospital in Toronto and in the services of many other necessary organizations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' NOTICES OF MOTIONS
speechtext: The cardiac unit.

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' NOTICES OF MOTIONS
speechtext:
My friend, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), mentions the cardiac unit at the Ottawa Civic Hospital. We face almost a crisis in some of those areas, and we must think about this very carefully and find some answers.
Solutions must be found, but without relying primarily on government grants because sometimes the views of governments on particular activities do not coincide with the views of the leaders and members of voluntary organizations. I think we need a new approach, and if government has a role to play in all this, its role is to create an atmosphere in which people will be enticed to give and support volunteer organizations. I think government has the role of providing incentive for people to give. If this was done, I believe certain things would happen. There would be greater self-reliance on the part of voluntary organizations. There would be enhanced sensitivity and accountability on the part of voluntary organizations to the constituencies they serve. There would be greater participation by citizens in voluntary organizations because, as all of us who are in politics know, the fact of the matter is that a donation from someone usually means a commitment from that person to participate as well. There would be an increase in the number and capacity of voluntary organizations to provide social and economic support to worth-while activities. There would be a diversified financial base.
Given the fact that it is a Friday afternoon, I suggest to the government as kindly as I can, that perhaps once again in the budget we missed a great opportunity to do what this motion would do or what the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton South would have done. Either one of those propositions would be acceptable to me. One would be less expensive to the government than the other, but the basic proposition is to do away with the automatic charitable donation of $100, which does not entice people to give to voluntary organizations, but in fact serves the administrative process more than anything else. It is a matter of the pen claiming the deduction rather than the pen writing the contribution cheque.
The contribution cheque is the purpose behind this motion, and it was the purpose behind the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton South. This would be an encouragement the government could give. I know that the parliamentary secretary or whoever will be speaking today has figures to indicate the costs of my motion and, likely, the cost to the government

February 12, 1982
Income Tax
of the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton South. I do not say this proposal would not cost the government revenue. It would cost the government a tremendous amount of revenue, but this would be a donation by government through a change in the statute. The government would provide an incentive to give. If people do not give, they cannot claim the deduction. Under this proposal the government would ally itself, in terms of the over-all delivery of social services, with volunteer organizations of all kinds, which would be strengthened and enhanced both in terms of the things they could engage in and in terms of their nature. It is in a real way the give and take system.
I think this House should consider this proposal. I hope at the end of this day this motion will be considered by the House not as a direction to government to act, because it is not framed that way, but as a direction to government to consider this proposal as well as the proposal of the hon. member for Edmonton South, which I had the privilege to second.
I have never found anyone in government or in any political party who disagrees in principle with this motion and the idea behind it. Everyone agrees that the current system is inequitable and provides virtually no incentive to people to be generous. The current system causes, at the same time, a considerable expenditure of public funds, because many of the services voluntary organizations cannot provide, but which are necessary, must be provided. I believe the problem is lack of political will to act. It was with that idea of generating that will that the government under the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), when he was prime minister, proposed a parliamentary task force, as it is called today, or a select committee on the voluntary sector. That proposal stood in my name as the then president of the Privy Council. I was very proud that it happened that way. It would have permitted a committee of the House, as was done in the case of the disabled and in so many other cases, to focus public attention on the requirements of the voluntary sector of the community.
If this debate today will simulate the same desire on the part of the government to propose that kind of special task force, as they like to call it, under the auspices of this Parliament where the voluntary sector and those in the community who depend on it can come and tell us what is required and we can urge the government to make the changes, then I would be very happy. 1 promise that I will not accuse the government of stealing our idea; I would applaud it for that! I would applaud it for its wisdom in the circumstances and, to the extent it was possible for me to do so, I would applaud it from one end of the country to the other.
I think it is important that we not forget, in a period of restraint when government is drawing back and services are being cut back, that there are still needs that have to be served and people who are disadvantaged in the community. There are still groups that are socially and culturally disadvantaged. If the job of government is anything at all, it is to instil in people the will to do public good. If by changes in the tax
system we can remove the disincentive to giving to charities rather than merely claiming the exemption, then I think we will have advanced the cause of humanity in the country and the delivery of social services. If I may say so, we will have done a service by enhancing and helping the government as it moves into this difficult time of restraint.
There is a large army of volunteers out there, Mr. Speaker. It is an army for good. Its will, its sense of what is right, its sense of what is needed should be harnessed. It is within the hands of the government to do that. All of us agree that something should be done now.
The national volunteer organizations and their constituent members would be delighted to see agreement with this motion and the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton South. They would be delighted to see some action by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Indeed, they would be very pleased if we should begin an examination of their importance and their place in society.
If that is the result of the work of the hon. member for Edmonton South and the public consideration of this motion, I will be very pleased. I will support and applaud the government if it will only consider this from the point of view of the appointment of what it calls a parliamentary task force. The need is there and we must create the will and the understanding in the community. We must give those National Voluntary Organizations in the community not just a voice here, but a place here.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' NOTICES OF MOTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has indicated, the charitable organizations in our country do a fantastic job of serving a need that could never be served by government at any economic cost. They meet the requirements of a large body of Canadians who require services in social and economic areas. We are in the debt of the voluntary sector for the services it provides.
The motion put forward by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton and an earlier motion by the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) are somewhat different. I would like to go into some of the concerns that I have with these motions.
The National Voluntary Organization has been making representations to government for some time to modify the existing provisions that apply to charitable donations in order to enhance the incentive for people to give. They have put forward a somewhat different proposal than those put forward by the two members opposite.
Earlier last year in my role as parliamentary secretary to the minister I was asked to examine the possibility of pulling together the diverse interests and recommendations made with regard to charitable giving to see how we could enhance them within the fiscal restraints of the government so that there
February 12, 1982

could be some resolution of the differences that have existed among members of Parliament and the volunteer community.
We worked with other parliamentarians in a small group and with people from the voluntary sector to try to come to grips with this question. At the moment 1 understand that this issue is in the hands of the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) who is putting together a final proposal to be presented either as a white paper or as proposals for legislation in the not too distant future.
This is the second time in this session that we have had a motion dealing with tax deductions for charitable donations. Certainly we all recognize that it is a very important area and one which should be dealt with at the earliest possible moment. There is great interest in and concern about the subject, and this is reflected in the motion we are debating today and in the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton South which was debated on June 9, 1980. These interests and concerns are shared by the government and there has been an ongoing review of the whole question of government initiative for charitable giving, and of the most appropriate form that this incentive could take. There is general agreement that some form of incentive is necessary and justifiable but there are different views on the nature and extent of the incentive and how it should be provided. Today I should like to review some of the considerations that must be taken into account and to look at some of the approaches that might be taken to resolve this issue.
First of all, there are several key principles that must be taken into account in any consideration. One involves equity, which is particularly important in our tax system. Any incentive that we provide through the tax system should seek to deal equitably among taxpayers and this principle, of course, was put forward rather forcefully in the recent budget.
In addition, the incentive should be as effective as possible in relation to its cost to the treasury. In other words, we should try to ensure that the money being put forward in the form of a tax expenditure-that is, dollars not collected by the treasury, that money forgone by the treasury that is naturally picked up by other taxpayers-is allocated in the most efficient manner possible to the charitable organizations in the country.
Another important consideration is that we continue to respect the pluralistic nature of our society. The great variety of our voluntary agencies is important to our social fabric and we should seek to give free rein to this aspect of charitable organizations.
A further consideration that we should bear in mind is the administrative costs and convenience of the approach that we select. There are differences in approach. Some individuals would say that the federal government or a level of government should enter into a direct expenditure program to fund charitable organizations. That is one of the options that have been put forward. Another would be through the tax system, while others could be to use a method similar to the one we have now with an automatic deduction in the tax system to avoid the administrative costs of providing tax receipts for
Income Tax
every donation. On the other hand, it would mean that certain individuals may claim deductions for which no charitable donations were given in the first place.
If we look carefully at the standard $100 deduction which is in place now, we realize that it is actually a disincentive to giving, because an individual who gives nothing has a tax reduction of some amount depending on his marginal tax rate. If his marginal tax rate is 25 per cent, by not giving anything and simply claiming the $100 deduction, he is $25 ahead of the game. Therefore, the first dollar given to a charitable organization reduces that $25. In the first $25 the individual is losing twice; he is giving $1 to a charitable organization and is giving up $1 of tax saving. It is actually a disincentive. I am quite concerned that a standard deduction, which does not require substantiation in the form of a receipt, is actually a disincentive to giving. We would probably see a higher level of charitable donations if we simply eliminated the $100 deduction altogether.
The other question raised by the hon. member's motion suggests that we should have a $100 deduction for medical expenses. There is a slight problem here because the standard rule in the tax law now is that the $100 deduction is for medical expenses and charitable donations. This deduction was really included for administrative purposes, so that people would not have to attach $1 or $2 receipts to their tax forms and send them in. In that event Revenue Canada people would be required to go through the various receipts. We said that the first $100 was automatic whether one gave anything or not. Given that we now have a computerized system which is becoming more sophisticated all the time, it is not beyond my imagination to ask why we could not have standard receipts that are machine readable. This would eliminate a great deal of administrative bother. Employees of Revenue Canada would actually be able to check the individual receipts as they came in, and it would eliminate the disincentive to which I referred earlier.
I have some problems with regard to the medical deduction. As I said, the standard in the present tax system is that an individual can claim medical expenses over and above 3 per cent of his income. The reason for this is that we have one of the finest medical insurance systems in the world, in the form of our hospitalization or medicare. As a result it was thought that only those expenses over and above relatively small expenditures for medical care should be deductible from tax, and that it should be greater than 3 per cent of income. If the first $100 deduction was allowed for medical expenses, we would have a double standard. The first $100 would be deductible, and everything between $100 and 3 per cent of income would not be deductible, and everything over 3 per cent, substantiated by receipts, would be deductible. Given the fact that we have such a very effective medical insurance and medical security system in the country, quite frankly I see no reason for leaving the standard deduction of $100 for medical purposes. If a person has legitimate medical expenses, that is one thing, but if he has good health and no legitimate medical

February 12, 1982

expenses during the year, why should he be able to write off $100 just because it is in the tax system? I am of the opinion that we should eliminate the $100 deduction altogether, and then in Parliament or in committee we could look at the question as to whether there should be additional incentives to charitable giving over and above the fact that charitable donations are deductible from income for tax purposes.
Then of course the question arises as to whether it is adequate incentive or whether we should become involved in an incentive program such as the one put forward by NVO. That organization argues that the present system is an inequitable method of rewarding charitable givings. The suggestion is that a person in the 25 per cent marginal tax bracket receives the benefit of a $25 tax saving, whereas a person in the 50 per cent tax bracket receives a $50 savings. The notion of equity has been called into question in terms of different individuals with different tax brackets receiving different incentives from the public purse for charitable donations. As a result NVO indicated that instead of using a deduction system, it would prefer to see a tax credit whereby, for example, an individual would receive a 50 per cent tax credit. If he donated $100, then he could deduct $50 from his tax payable at the end of the year. This would mean that everyone would receive exactly the same benefit from the contribution, whether their marginal tax rate was 10 per cent or 50 per cent, which is now the top bracket.
Clearly this raises some problems because the top marginal tax rate in the present system is 50 per cent and the average marginal tax rate is less than that. For any given level of donation, obviously the contribution in the form of tax revenue forgone would be much higher under a 50 per cent tax credit than in the present situation. As I understand the current situation, the revenue forgone from the personal and corporate tax system was somewhere in the range of $425 million for the year 1980. Therefore, if we used a 50 per cent tax credit it would not only increase the value of donations given now, it would probably be a substantial incentive to increase donations, and the cost to the treasury could be well in excess of $1 million, although this is only a guesstimate on my part.
For example, if the average marginal tax rate of Canadians was 30 per cent and the tax credit becomes 50 per cent, there is an automatic 40 per cent increase in cost. Of course 40 per cent of $425 million is almost another $200 million, so there is $625 million. If there was an additional incentive effect it would be between $625 million and $1 billion, somewhere in that range. I am not sure how much it would be, but certainly it would be a substantial increase.
At a time of fiscal restraint the government is reluctant to undertake any major program, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated on a number of occasions in answer to questions posed over the last couple of weeks. Requests were put forward to increase expenditures over and above the level of the envelopes now, such as to increase the expenditures for job creation and to increase assistance for home owners, farmers, fishermen and so on. The minister has indicated that he is not prepared to do this outside the present
structure and fiscal plan and, as a result, I think he would be quite reluctant to move to a tax credit scheme or some similar scheme which would involve major increases in expenditures from revenue.
It is a very important point which we as parliamentarians should consider. I have raised in the House before that the notion of tax expenditures is an extremely important concept for us to deal with, because we have an expenditure plan which must be financed. If we make conscious decisions not to collect revenue from someone, then someone else or everyone else is required to pay higher taxes than they would otherwise pay to fund the expenditure plan. This is because someone is not paying as much as he would without that tax expenditure being in place. Every time we put a tax expenditure in place we are causing other Canadians to carry a heavier burden than otherwise. It is a very important concept. I tend to think of tax expenditures as just another form of direct expenditures. In one case the government spends taxpayers' money, in the other case the government decides not to collect from some taxpayers. From my perspective the effect is the same in terms of the burden on the taxpayers.
With that said, I would suggest to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton that it is a very worthy cause he has put forward. I can tell him that the government is actively developing policies in this particular area right now. Proposals will come forward to deal with the voluntary organization question.
I am sure as parliamentarians we can come to a resolution of this problem that will be satisfactory not only to the voluntary organizations but satisfactory from the point of view of the taxpayer in that we will be providing the assistance that all Canadians wish to provide to the voluntary sector in the most effecient and effective way possible.

Mr. Speaker. 1 wish to speak in support of the general direction of this proposal for a bookkeeping improvement in the way that charitable donations are handled. While we are considering the subject, we should be willing to give the whole matter of charitable donations a very thorough rethinking.
As times have changed the role of charitable donations should also change. It is now possible that low-income people who are almost by definition the object of charitable giving can do a great deal for themselves. In some ways they can do it better than can be done by those who are the traditional source of charity. We have developed all kinds of techniques for co-operatives. For example, co-operative joint self-education in poor communities and various kinds of mutual help in neighbourhoods. for which a certain amount ol tinancial assistance would be most useful. The question is who controls this? If these local self-help organizations have to be controlled by outside do-gooders, by ladies bountiful, men or women, whatever sex, or by academics who are primarily interested in doing research, the benefit to them is very questionable.
I live in the Kensington area of Toronto which, according to a former member of the provincial legislature, Allan Gross-

man, has been studied probably more than any other part of Canada.

The Kensington area is just about a mile from the University of Toronto. Every first-year student of sociology, economics, politics, etc., are told to study the Kensington area. It would be cheating to use the study done the previous year or 20 years ago, so people are always coming around to ask us questions. At first there seems to be ready help for local groups and things such as community centres, but students are required to use this practical experience to advance their credits. They are not really able to give free voluntary help to a local group.
Low-income people who need this help have shown a great deal of ability to govern their own organization if allowed to. It would be very useful to have the tax system changed so as to allow them to control the charities that serve them rather than having the charities be instruments by which people of middle and upper-income control the lower-income people.
One way of doing this would be first to make sure that basic services are not treated as matters of charity. The basic services are funded on the tax base or within a particular service, institution or charitable activity. A certain base is funded on the tax base and perhaps extras then are funded by additional charitable donations.
There are many groups which do not yet have adequate funding from the tax base. They have to go cap in hand every year for another grant from the municipal council and another grant from the provincial government and another grant from the federal government. These people spend a large part of their year just trying to make sure that they will still be in business in the future. I am thinking of rape crisis centres which have demonstrated that they are necessary but have great difficulty getting funding. Hostels for battered wives, with or without their battered children, exist. They have proven their worth by the number of people they have to turn away. Yet these hostels are still extremely short of funds. Those that do exist are in a most precarious financial state.
In our large cities we need youth drop-in centres to give youth, who. for w hatever reason ureperhapsalicnated from their homes, if they have homes, some kind of social group around which to orient. This type of thing is desperately needed. It should be provided on a secure basis so that the director and the volunteer board of such a group does not always have to be skewing its work in order to be able to go to a government and show they have such and such a case load and such and such a success rate on a short-term basis which makes basic and long-term work very difficult to do. It would be much better if the work of these groups was accountable in a broad way on the tax base rather than the groups being treated as either strictly private charities or as hybrid outfits who have to beg money from private sources or beg money by annual or semi-annual grants from all levels of government.
The second way that we should make this change is by using a tax credit instead of a tax deduction. The tax credit would
