give recognition and appropriate reward to low-income people who give to these things instead of making this a traditional tax haven only for high-income people. Let them have dollar for dollar credit for what they give. If the high-income people wish to give more then they will be credited accordingly. But the low-income people, especially those who do not have enough income to enjoy the privilege of paying income tax, cannot get anything from a tax deduction. But they should be recognized through the system of tax credit.
Finally, and the most important change that would have to be made, would be in the charitable organizations legislation. It must be recognized in order to include clearly and positively the concept of an advocacy group. It should include advocacy groups dedicated and openly committed to trying to produce social changes. We may not all agree on what kinds of social changes are wanted, but we could agree that any organization that seriously tries to put forward a social goal and works toward that goal should be able to solicit donations on the basis of an advocacy group as a charitable organization.
That is already done for three well-known advocacy groups who do not agree about the kind of change they want in this country. I belong to one called the New Democratic Party. My colleagues to the right belong to another and my colleagues opposite, if any of them had stayed around, belong to another. We do not agree exactly about what kinds of changes we want. We are all recognized as being members of a kind of advocacy group. We all have tax credits as a basis for raising our donations. This should not be limited to people running for public office federally or provincially. It should be extended to people who are going to do the other kinds of very necessary work for changing our society.
I am thinking of, for example, consumer organizations and groups such as native friendship centres which have been directly threatened by the loss of their charitable status if they dare to suggest that the Department of Indian Affairs does not always do things right, whether it be the federal or provincial department. They should not be threatened and hampered in carrying out their mandate on behalf of the native peoples of Canada by being faulted as charitable organizations for doing something for which political parties praise themselves, namely, trying to change the laws of this country.
Community centres in Toronto have often been attacked in the same way. They have been told they cannot get political. If the supporters of a community centre do not wish to give money because they do not like the activities of that centre, then the centre will fold. But it should not be in the power of government to say, because your community centre opposed the expressway that the city government happened to like, we do not think you should have your charitable status. That has not been said explicitly, so far, but it has been at times hinted at and we should revise the act so as to make clear that any social group in the neighbourhood should have the right to advocate the things the neighbourhood needs without having to fear for their charitable status.

There are many kinds of poor people's organizations. Many of them have not registered as charities, not only because it takes a little money, a little legal advice, and a little organization for which some poor people do not have the training; but also because of the nature of what they are trying to do, trying to change life for poor people, and for some in this country that is an unsatisfactory goal. They do not want the lives of the poor changed. They are able to organize their own charities in many cases, and the poor should be able to organize theirs.
For example, I am thinking, even of such middle groups as the Children's Aid in certain areas which, although it is a traditional group, has often entered into advocacy work, for example in Toronto, by advocating that we need better and more low-income housing, yet they have been criticized for "getting political". Who is it that criticizes them? The politicians.
Some politicians do not like someone encroaching on their monopoly so they say to Children's Aid, you are supposed to rescue the victims of bad housing but you are not supposed to say it is bad housing that made victims of them. They should be enabled to defend the people for whom they are charged as social guardians. They should be able to speak up and say what are the causes of so many broken families, so many disoriented children in our big cities. The chief reason the Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto pointed its finger was the unnecessary shortage of low-income housing in Metro Toronto. They were very much criticized for getting into that.
Tenants' organizations should be able to defend themselves. They should be able to fund themselves as charitable organizations, provided their books, like those of any other charitable organization, are open and their goals are open. Those organizations that I know of are quite willing to do that. They have nothing to hide. It is the landlords who like to keep their books secret.
There are all kinds of ethnic groups and interpreter services who would like to speak for and defend the interests of the immigrant groups they serve. However, they are hampered and hindered by the fear that if they speak up on behalf of those people, many of them low-income and disadvantaged people, they might lose their grants and be unable to continue the service. Of course, we have the interesting situation, which I believe has already been noted here some months past, where an educational publication has been attacked by the government and deprived, at least temporarily, of its charitable status on the grounds that it represents a certain biased point of view. I refer to a magazine called Dimension. On the other hand, an outfit like the Fraser Institute, which is equally biased-

Yes, as my colleague says, hardly charitable in the ordinary sense of the word. That institute can get tax benefits. Then there is an organization which purports to be religious and gets tax deductions for that reason, and carries on its main public activity by trying to destroy certain trustees in our educational system around Metro Toronto. 1 speak of Renaissance. That organization funds vicious and misleading, in fact outright lying propaganda from time to time with money given as charitable donations and recognized as such.
So, in fact we do recognize advocacy, whether it is by political parties, certain religious groups, or certain conservative minded educational groups. Why not be consistent and let the poor also have their advocacy groups and have the same chance to move this country ahead; the same chance that is given to certain other and much more well-heeled groups which would hold this country back. I would hope when this is considered further we will really try to revise the whole concept of the charitable donation system in our tax laws and make it as available to low-income people as it is now to upper-income people.
